summary_html: Agency places a child with **relatives or kin caregivers** instead of non-relative foster care. Federal law favors kinship care as least-restrictive, family-preserving placement.

key_cases.holding: The agency need not prove that no suitable relative was available before permanent custody may be granted; the availability of a placement that would avoid termination is one relevant factor in the R.C. 2151.414(D) weighing, not a controlling one.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Ohio holding on how much weight a proposed kinship placement carries against permanent custody.
key_cases.quote: The statute does not make the availability of a placement that would not require a termination of parental rights an all-controlling factor.

key_cases.holding: An adjudication that a child is abused, neglected or dependent implicitly determines the unsuitability of both custodial and noncustodial parents, so no separate parental-unsuitability finding is required before a juvenile court awards legal custody to a nonparent, though the adjudication does not permanently foreclose a later change of custody.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling authority permitting a kinship or nonrelative legal custody award after adjudication without a further unsuitability finding.
key_cases.quote: abuse, neglect, or dependency adjudications implicitly involve a determination of the unsuitability of the child's parents

key_cases.holding: In a private custody dispute a trial court must make an on-the-record parental unsuitability determination before awarding legal custody of a child to a nonparent, and that determination is made once, at the time of the legal custody hearing.
key_cases.relevance: When kin seek custody outside an abuse, neglect or dependency case, Hockstok requires an express unsuitability finding first.
key_cases.quote: A parent should be given only one unsuitability determination, which should come at the time of the legal custody hearing.

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of Ohio, Tenth Appellate District
key_cases.holding: The juvenile court erred as a matter of law by transferring jurisdiction over an Indian child to the tribal court despite a parent's objection and without addressing 25 U.S.C. 1911(b) good cause, and it must hold an evidentiary hearing on whether good cause exists to deviate from the 25 U.S.C. 1915(b) placement preferences and on the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It requires an evidentiary finding of good cause before an Ohio court departs from ICWA's extended-family and tribal placement preferences.
key_cases.quote: The juvenile court erred as a matter of law in disregarding the parental veto, disregarding the good cause provision of 25 U.S.C. 1911(b), and transferring jurisdiction to GRIC's tribal court.

key_cases.holding: In a juvenile court custody action between a parent and a nonparent under R.C. 2151.23(A)(2), a parent may be denied custody only on a finding, supported by a preponderance of the evidence, of abandonment, contractual relinquishment of custody, total inability to provide care or support, or other unsuitability meaning that an award of custody would be detrimental to the child; the judgment was reversed because the trial court made no unsuitability finding.
key_cases.relevance: This is the source decision for the unsuitability requirement that Hockstok restates, and it enumerates the only four grounds on which kin or another nonparent may displace a parent outside a dependency case.
key_cases.quote: a preponderance of the evidence indicates abandonment, contractual relinquishment of custody, total inability to provide care or support, or that the parent is otherwise unsuitable

key_cases.case_name: Pittman v. Cuyahoga Cty. Dept. of Children & Family Servs.
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of immunity to an Ohio caseworker, holding her absolutely immune for the juvenile complaint and the affidavits she filed in her advocacy capacity, and qualifiedly immune on the father's substantive and procedural due process claims because Ohio law places responsibility for placement decisions and for notice of custody proceedings on the juvenile court rather than on the caseworker.
key_cases.relevance: A parent or relative whose caregiver-approval process is halted has no damages claim against the caseworker for that decision, because the placement determination is the court's to make — the source decision Brent applies.
key_cases.quote: it is the juvenile court's responsibility to ensure that Pittman received adequate notice of the custody proceedings
